Which ROC filings a private company owes each year, and when

RESOLVED THAT ₹13,50,000 be spent in 2026–27 on a science laboratory and computer room at the Zilla Parishad school, Mahalunge, through a registered education trust.

tasks.title: Check the minutes and the register
tasks.prompt: Read the index, each meeting’s minutes and the register of directors’ contracts; the company’s master data is under Other papers. Mark each paper Fine or Exception and pick what is wrong. Your calls go to Snehal when you move on.

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your calls on the minutes and the register to Snehal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change them after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Snehal. You can read your calls but not change them.

hints: Count days: from each meeting to its date of entry in the book, and from one meeting to the next. Then read who was present and who disclosed what.
Some decisions count only when passed at a Board meeting, and borrowing is one. Every director also discloses interests at the first meeting of each year.

options.label: More than 120 days between two meetings
No quorum for the business done
Minutes entered in the book after 30 days
A director’s disclosure of interest is missing
An interested director took part in the decision
Borrowing approved without a Board meeting
Register entry differs from the Board’s approval
Register not signed at the next Board meeting

fields.label: Your note for the file
fields.placeholder: For example: 3 of 4 present; entered 18 days after

items.label: Index · the year’s meetings
items.note: Index: five meetings in 2026–27. From meeting 90 the gaps run 97, 52, 35, 90 and 90 days, and 18 May is 97 days after 10 February. None is over 120. Fine.

items.label: Meeting 91 · 19 May 2026
items.note: Meeting 91: the first meeting of 2026–27, all four present, but the minutes note MBP-1 from only three. Nandini’s disclosure is missing, and every director gives one at the first meeting of each year. Exception.

items.label: Meeting 92 · 10 July 2026
items.note: Meeting 92: only Amol in the room and Nandini on video. With four directors the quorum is two, and video counts. So term loan II was approved by resolution at a valid meeting. Fine.

items.label: Meeting 93 · 14 August 2026
items.note: Meeting 93: all four present, the June quarter’s results approved by resolution, the loan drawn and the machine noted, and the minutes entered 27 days after the meeting. Fine.

items.label: Meeting 94 · 12 November 2026
items.note: Meeting 94: the minutes went into the book on 24 December, 42 days after the meeting; the limit is 30. Sejal Joglekar’s contract is fine: she disclosed her interest and left the room, and no other director is interested. Exception.

items.label: Meeting 95 · 10 February 2027
items.prompt: With the resolution passed by circulation that this meeting noted.
items.note: Meeting 95: the cash-credit renewal was approved by circular resolution on 22 December and only noted here. A cash-credit arrangement is borrowing in the Act’s own words, and borrowing needs a resolution at a meeting. Exception.

items.label: Register · directors’ contracts
items.note: Register: the entry for Sejal Joglekar’s contract says ₹60,000; the 12 November minutes approve ₹6,00,000. It was placed before the next meeting and signed, as it should be, but the figure is wrong. Exception.

tasks.title: List the year’s ROC filings and their dates
tasks.prompt: Roll Mrunal’s tracker forward to the filings for 2026–27. For each form, say whether it falls due for this year and, if it does, by when. The AGM is proposed for 28 September 2027. Your list goes to Snehal when you move on.

lockOnLeave.ask: Hand your filing list to Snehal?
lockOnLeave.note: You can’t change it after this.
lockOnLeave.done: Handed to Snehal. You can read your list but not change it.

hints: Don’t copy last year’s tracker line by line. Ask what triggers each form: the AGM, a fixed date, an appointment, a half-year, or the size of the company.
Read Mahesh’s mail against his own ageing list. Who counts for MSME-1: micro suppliers only, or micro and small?

options.label: Within 60 days of the half-year’s end

fields.label: Your note for the calendar
fields.placeholder: For example: what sets the date this year

items.label: AOC-4 · financial statements
items.note: AOC-4: the 2026–27 financial statements go to the ROC within 30 days of the AGM. With the AGM on 28 September, that means by late October. Due.

items.label: MGT-7 · annual return
items.note: MGT-7: the annual return goes in within 60 days of the AGM, so by late November. Tamhini files MGT-7 because it is not a small company. Due.

items.label: MGT-7A · annual return
items.note: MGT-7A is the annual return of small companies and one person companies. Tamhini has ₹25 crore of paid-up capital, more than any small company can have, so it files MGT-7. Not due.

items.label: ADT-1 · auditors’ appointment
items.note: ADT-1 goes in within 15 days of an auditor’s appointment, not every year. We were appointed at the 2023 AGM until the end of the 2028 AGM, so nothing is due this year. Not due.

items.label: DIR-3 KYC · the four directors
items.note: DIR-3 KYC used to be yearly. Since 31 March 2026 it has been once in three years: all four filed in September 2025, so next by 30 June 2028, unless a director’s mobile, email or address changes. Not due.

items.label: DPT-3 · return of deposits
items.note: DPT-3 goes in by 30 June every year, and Mrunal files it with our certificate. The return as on 31 March 2027 is due by 30 June 2027. Due.

items.label: MSME-1 · October 2026 – March 2027
items.note: MSME-1: Mahesh looked only at micro suppliers. Small enterprises count too: Kudalwadi was owed ₹14,36,705 beyond 45 days at 31 March. His ageing also came before Shirur’s stale cheque was written back, so Shirur’s ₹44,660 counts as well. Due by 30 April, and missed.

items.label: PAS-6 · October 2026 – March 2027
items.note: PAS-6: a private company that is not small files it each half-year, within 60 days, and the tracker shows Tamhini’s last two. The half-year to 31 March 2027 is due by 30 May. Due.

items.label: MGT-14 · Board resolutions on borrowing
items.note: MGT-14: a private company does not file its Board resolutions on borrowing or on approving the accounts with the ROC. Not due.

tasks.title: Draft the note to Mrunal
tasks.prompt: Snehal wants one note to Mrunal Deo, Tamhini’s company secretary, with your points from the minutes, the register and the tracker. Pick the right line for each point.
hints: Fix each problem at its source, never by changing a date or a paper after the event. The 18 May meeting is where the Board can put things on record.

options.text: So please show Shirur only, as the return covers micro suppliers alone.
options.why: It covers micro and small enterprises alike, so Kudalwadi’s dues go in beside Shirur’s, and the return was due by 30 April.

options.text: So the return was due by 30 April. Please file it now.
options.why: Small enterprises count as much as micro ones. The date has gone, so it goes in now, before anything else.

options.text: So please show both in the April to September return, due by 31 October.
options.why: Wrong half-year. Those dues were outstanding in October to March, and the October to March return was due by 30 April.

options.text: As 18 May is the first meeting of 2027–28, please place all four MBP-1s for the year, hers included, before the Board.
options.why: Every director discloses at the first meeting of each year. The 2026–27 one can’t be put right now; the 2027–28 one can be, on 18 May.

options.text: As hers is the one missing, please have her sign an MBP-1 dated 19 May 2026 now and file it with that meeting’s papers.
options.why: Never. A back-dated disclosure is a false record. What is late stays late; we get the next one right.

options.text: As the fund’s nominee has no interests of her own to disclose, nothing more is needed from her, this year or next.
options.why: Every director discloses, nominee or not. A fund’s nominee often sits on other boards too, and that is exactly what MBP-1 asks about.

options.text: The Chairman has signed them, so the date of entry no longer matters and the book can stay as it is.
options.why: It matters. Minutes are to be kept within 30 days of the meeting, and a signature does not change when they went in.

options.text: The limit is 30 days. Please keep to it for the coming meetings, starting with 18 May.
options.why: A late entry can’t be undone. Say it plainly and keep the next ones on time.

options.text: The limit is 30 days. Please rewrite the date of entry as 10 December, so that the book shows 28 days.
options.why: Never. Changing the date of entry falsifies the minutes book, and the minutes are the evidence of the meeting.

options.text: It has all four directors’ approval, so it stands as a Board resolution and the file is complete.
options.why: Approvals on a circular do not make a meeting, and borrowing needs a resolution passed at one.

options.text: It was not passed at a meeting, so please ask the bank to stop drawings on the limit until the Board passes one.
options.why: Too far. The plant runs on that limit. What is missing is the Board’s resolution at a meeting, and the Board meets on 18 May.

options.text: It is borrowing, which needs a resolution passed at a Board meeting, so please put the renewal on the 18 May agenda.
options.why: A circular resolution is not enough for borrowing. The 18 May meeting can pass it the way the law wants, and the file will show both.

options.text: As the register must match the minutes, please correct the entry and place it before the Board on 18 May.
options.why: The register has to match what the Board approved, and a corrected entry goes before the next meeting to be signed.

options.text: As the two papers must agree, please change the 12 November minutes to ₹60,000, so that they match the register entry.
options.why: The other way round. The minutes are the record of what the Board decided; the register copies from them.

options.text: As the register is only for the company’s own use, the difference can stay, and nothing more is needed.
options.why: No. The law requires this register, and we read it to check contracts with directors. A wrong figure in it is a wrong record.

freeText.label: Your own line for the note

passNeeds.note: You need more of the seven calls on the minutes and the register right to pass.
You need more of the nine filing calls right to pass.

wrap.text: Four points in the minutes and the register, and one filing that slipped. The circular resolution matters most: borrowing needs a Board meeting, however many directors approve it. The note goes to Mrunal tomorrow, MSME-1 first, as it is already late.

wrapPartial.text: Four points in the minutes and the register, and one filing that slipped past the tracker. I’ll go through the note with you tomorrow morning, before anything goes to Mrunal.

wrapRetry.text: This file is mostly dates and names. Count the days from each meeting to its entry in the book, and between meetings. Check who was present, who disclosed and what was decided without a meeting. Then test each form against this year’s facts, not last year’s list.

model.intro: Four of the seven papers carry an exception: a disclosure missing at the first meeting of the year, minutes entered 42 days after the meeting, a borrowing approved by circular resolution, and a register entry one zero short. Of the nine forms, five fall due and four do not, and the MSME-1 for October to March was missed.

blocks.text: Read minutes twice: first for the law, then for the accounts, because a loan or a contract the Board approves has to show in the books or the notes.

principles: Minutes are the evidence of what the Board decided. Read them for the law and for the accounts.

interview.q: What do you look for when you read a company’s board minutes?
interview.checking: Whether you read minutes for the law and the accounts, or only look for signatures.
outline: For the law: a quorum, no gap over 120 days, and borrowing passed at meetings, not by circulation.
For the accounts: the loans, contracts and commitments the Board approved, which the books or notes must show.

interview.q: Which ROC filings does a private company make each year, and by when?
interview.checking: Whether you know the forms, what triggers each one, and the three-year KYC rule.
outline: AOC-4 within 30 days of the AGM; MGT-7, or MGT-7A if small, within 60; DPT-3 by 30 June.
ADT-1 on appointment; DIR-3 KYC every three years; MSME-1 half-yearly for micro and small dues past 45 days.
